extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary students, and critics studying methods of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on two contrasting novel-writing methods—panoramic (pictorial) versus scenic (dramatic)—and criteria for when to use each, how to handle unity, point of view, time, and climactic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic (pictorial) vs Scenic (dramatic) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the “panoramic” (pictorial) presentation—broad, retrospective survey of a landscape of life—and the “scenic” (dramatic) presentation—direct enactment of scenes where the reader watches the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panoramic: a continuous flow of leisurely, contemplative reminiscence; the whole is in view at once and the author’s mind/surge of memories governs the narrative. Scenic/dramatic: places the scene immediately before the reader and lets characters act with minimal authorial intervention. Choose the method appropriate to the story’s aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of panoramic method for impression-of-a-world subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The panoramic manner is right for stories whose point is an impression of a world, society, or time rather than a single central plot or complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject is 'an impression of manners' or 'a chapter in the career of well-to-do London,' a panoramic survey that marshals many incidents for effect is preferable to concentrating on an intricately woven intrigue (example: Thackeray's Vanity Fair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity via typicity and mass of life rather than intricate plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of a panoramic novel often derives from the fact that characters are strongly typical of their world and together create a single impression, not from tightly interlocked plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such works the 'light link' between characters suffices: the book becomes 'the story which they unite to tell.' Avoid forcing artificial plot connections when unity is intended to be pictorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of particular incidents to broad effect (foreshortening/generalizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: In panoramic writing, instances and occasions should be subordinated to the broad pictorial effect: brief hints, moments, or glimpses should illustrate and enrich the overall impression rather than be fully-exacted scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'a hint, a moment, a glance' to contribute to the picture; brush past details without over-particularizing so the stream of recollection flows and the general tone remains dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve dramatic enactment for moments that demand immediate embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the material culminates in a question whose force depends on witnessing events (a climax), the method demands direct, present action—i.e., a fully enacted scene before the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not summarize decisive climaxes; place them 'immediately before us' to provide the best possible warrant and prevent weakening the force of the answer (example: Becky’s catastrophe requires an enacted scene rather than retrospective account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare characters for independence to avoid theatrical/crude devices
rubrics_metrics.description: If a panoramic method has kept characters mostly as figures of the author’s vision, they may be ill-prepared to carry a full dramatic scene, leading to forced theatricality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid neglecting earlier rendering of characters in immediate terms; give them enough groundwork to act convincingly without 'forcing their note' or resorting to crude devices at the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dissipating potential dramatic occasions within panorama
rubrics_metrics.description: A panoramic author may 'waste' occasions that should be dramatic by subsuming them in picture-making, resulting in scenes that leave no image or effect (e.g., the Waterloo ball in Vanity Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize historic or pivotal events that the story 'needs' and give them concrete enactment rather than treating them as mere decorative patches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence must be accounted for (authenticate the point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic mode tends to foreground the narrator’s omniscient eye; if that eye remains unaccounted for the book may feel inconclusive or externally dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the knowing mind/objective spectator part of the book (i.e., 'dramatize the seeing eye') so the narrator’s authority is verifiable within the fiction and the work is self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blending of perspectives to minimize intrusive narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Blending the author's vision with a character's point of view (as Flaubert does with Emma) can make authorial intervention unobtrusive and give the appearance that the character’s vision governs the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ subtle alignment of narrator and character perspectives so that the narrator does not seem to dominate the tale; this can avoid the constant reminder of an external telling-mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture vs drama: control reader’s relation to the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture (panoramic) makes the reader face the storyteller and listen; drama makes the reader watch the story itself with the author effaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you want the reader conscious of the narrator (companionable telling) or absorbed in the scene (dramatic watching) and use technique (voice, focalization, stage setting) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effacement of the author in dramatic/scenic method
rubrics_metrics.description: In the scenic/dramatic method the author should minimize signs of his own judgement so the scene appears to tell itself; the novelist approximates the dramatist by leaving the characters and events to make their impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide immediate, literal detail and let the motion of life occupy the reader; avoid frequent authorial asides or summarizing that draw attention back to the storyteller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of chronology and focus to create 'time-pictures'
rubrics_metrics.description: To represent time as tranquillity rather than movement (a 'time-picture'), the novelist may roam to and fro in narrative, delay and return, and shift focus so the sense of stored-up time deepens the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use leisurely play with chronology and shifting focus (close and far) to create layers of time in place of sequential movement (example: Castlewood in Esmond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and use of vivid, piercing flashes of revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional sharp, unforgettable moments (flashes of revelation) within a panoramic book can supply dramatic intensity, but they remain fragments unless integrated or deliberately enacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ these flashes (a child's face, a cathedral choir) to crystallize impression, yet recognize their fragmentary nature and consider when full enactment would better serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence about omniscient convention—make the narrator accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: The omniscient-author convention permits universal knowledge, but overuse or unaccounted assertion of that knowledge invites questioning and weakens the novel's internal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either restrain omniscience or incorporate it into the book's terms (verify the point of view internally) to avoid a sense that the narrative depends on an external, unverifiable authority.
